Chapter 9: The Sleepwalkers—How Ordinary Choices Led to Catastrophe.
When you look back, it’s pretty easy to search for villains—people who wanted war, who plotted and schemed for their own gain. But the story of 1914? It’s a lot more complicated than that.
Most of the folks in power didn’t actually want disaster. They were hoping to avoid it, or at least keep it under control. Still, step by step, they made choices that led the world toward catastrophe.
In those government offices, decisions happened fast, often with only half the facts. Leaders relied on their own instincts, the advice of their closest aides, and the so-called logic of alliances. They figured that flexing their muscles—making threats or bold moves—would keep the peace. But here’s what really happened: every move got answered with a countermove, every warning sparked a new demand.
The whole system was fragile. Think about it: tangled alliances, pressure from the public, and military plans that didn’t make room for slowing down. All that made compromise nearly impossible. And once the crisis got rolling, stopping it became even harder. Every side was terrified that if they paused—even for a moment—it would spell disaster, or look like weakness.
Regular people were swept up in the drama, too. Crowds cheered for war. Newspapers pushed leaders to take action. The pressure to do something—anything—just kept growing.
In the end, the leaders of Europe weren’t monsters, and they weren’t fools. They were just human—proud, nervous, and often totally overwhelmed by what was happening around them.
The real tragedy of 1914 is how much came down to pure chance—misunderstandings, missed messages, and this stubborn hope that maybe, just maybe, disaster could still be avoided.
The sleepwalkers of history weren’t evil. They were ordinary people, tangled in a web of their own making.
